profile.summary: Prosit Transformer predicts MS2 fragment intensities for a peptide using a transformer instead of the recurrent network of the original Prosit. It takes a peptide sequence with its precursor charge and collision energy and predicts the intensities of the six common ion series (singly, doubly and triply charged b and y ions). It is built by putting a prediction head on TAPE, a transformer trained on protein sequences, and fine-tuning it on the Prosit training data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: TAPE is a transformer autoencoder trained on Pfam protein sequences to fill in a missing residue. It has 12 attention layers of 768 hidden units and encodes the peptide into a 512-dimensional embedding. A Prosit-specific transformer with the same settings but nine attention layers decodes the combined embedding. A separate metadata layer, a two-layer perceptron of width 512, takes seven inputs: a six-dimensional one-hot charge state and the collision energy. Its output is combined with the peptide embedding before the decoder, and a two-layer prediction layer follows the decoder. Predicted negative intensities are set to zero, and ions that cannot exist for a peptide, because the charge or the length is too low, are set to -1 and excluded from similarity measurements.

The Prosit-specific transformer has the same parameter but consists of nine attention layers. The metadata layer is a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with two layers of size 512 units followed by a dropout rate of 0.1 each.
The TAPE model will encode the peptide into a 512-dimensional embedding.

we used layers for handling metadata consisting of the charge state of the spectrum and its collision energy (CE). The charge states range from one to six, represented as six-dimensional one-hot encoding.
Hence, the metadata layer has seven input nodes to account for the charge state and CE.
we set ions with a predicted negative intensity to zero, i.e., a negative intensity indicates an absent peak

Then a Prosit-specific Transformer will decode this combined embedding. Lastly, a two-layered multilayer perception (MLP) follows the decoding layer, serving as a prediction layer to predict the spectrum intensity.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is in the first author's repository, which has no licence file and no release. It installs with pip install -e . and uses the TAPE training command, and the README's notes say that downloading trained models is still a to-do, so no weights are published there. The training data are the Prosit HDF5 files from figshare, converted to LMDB; the paper says the converted LMDB files were deposited on figshare as well. A result therefore has to state which model the author trained and with which config file; the repository's example config is config/prositTransformer.json. This page read the repository at commit 36d788f5.

sections.title: How the benchmark used it
sections.body: PepSpecBench describes Prosit Transformer as a transformer of about 86M parameters and groups it with the sequence-centric models that predict b and y ion intensities by cleavage position and fragment charge. The paper itself states 164 million parameters. All six baselines were retrained on the benchmark data under backbone-disjoint splits, so the benchmark's figure describes its own retrained model.

quotes.text: 86M params), and AlphaPeptDeep
predict b/y-ion intensities indexed by cleavage position and fragment charge
All baselines are retrained on the benchmark data under the Backbone-Disjoint splits described above.
Prosit RNN contains 3 million parameters, while Prosit Transformer contains 164 million parameters, which gives the Transformer an unfair advantage.

strengths.text: It reuses a transformer already trained on protein sequences, so the authors say less data and much less training time are needed than training from scratch.

run_guide.summary: Install the repository, convert the Prosit data to LMDB and train the model, since no trained weights are published.
prerequisites: Python with pip, and NVIDIA Apex installed separately for training.
A CUDA GPU: the training command uses fp16 and the paper trained on A100 systems.
Disk space and time for the data conversion, which the README says takes about 20 hours for the training data.
No pretrained weights: the README lists downloadable models as a to-do.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/ekvall93/PrositTransformer
cd PrositTransformer
git checkout --detach 36d788f5c304fa67ceef57d1249c9878bb8c0a5d
steps.explanation: Clones the repository and pins it to the commit read for this page. The clone and checkout lines are added by Rewire.

quotes.text: pip install -e .

steps.title: Install
steps.explanation: The README's install command. It says everything required is installed except NVIDIA Apex, which only training needs.

quotes.text: pip install -e .
Everything that is required will be install except for Nvidia Apex.

steps.title: Download and convert the data
steps.explanation: Downloads the Prosit HDF5 files and converts one split to the LMDB format the TAPE framework reads. The same command is run per split.

quotes.text: bash downloadProsithdf5.sh

prosit2tape \
--prosit_hdf5_path /path/to/file.hdf5 \
--out_dir /path/to/data \
--split test

steps.title: Train the model
steps.explanation: The README's training command with its placeholder hyperparameter flags (batch size, learning rate, warmup steps, gradient accumulation, patience, epochs) left out by Rewire and the example config file from the repository filled in for the config path.

quotes.text:
tape-train \
    transformer \
    prosit_fragmentation \

--fp16 \
  --data_dir /path/to/data \
We have an example config file at config/prositTransformer.json

steps.title: Predict with the trained model
steps.explanation: The README's prediction command, taking the model trained in the previous step. It writes a result HDF5 file. The README also gives predictTF for a converted TensorFlow model.

quotes.text:
predictTorch \
--model /path/to/torch_model \
--lmdb /path/to/lmdb_data \
--split test \
--out_dir /path/to/predict_result
--prosit_hdf5_path /path/to/prosit/file_test.hdf5

outputs: A trained model in the output directory and, after the prediction step, a result HDF5 file of predicted intensities (torchResult.hdf5 or tfResult.hdf5) that the repository's validate and report scripts read.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
